title: Cooter

jokes.text: Jack lists his government responsibilities including 'the War on the Poor'
jokes.setup: Jack lists legitimate-sounding government portfolios: Homeland Security, extreme weather preparedness...
jokes.punchline: '...and the War on the Poor.' Then corrects to 'War on Poverty' only after Liz prompts him.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration — Jack Donaghy's patrician callousness toward the lower classes is core to his DNA. The slip is perfectly placed: sandwiched between real-sounding government portfolios so the punchline lands as genuine Freudian revelation rather than a setup joke. The beat where Liz has to correct him and he goes 'Yeah, okay, let's go with that' doubles down brilliantly. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Jack mentions 'the cryogenecists are already sharpening their head saws'
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Geiss might come out of his coma and name Jack as CEO.
jokes.punchline: 'The cryogenecists are already sharpening their head saws.'
jokes.explanation: Specific, vivid, absurd detail — 'head saws' is the perfect gross-specific word choice to make cryogenic freezing maximally grim. Delivered matter-of-factly by Jack which amplifies the dark comedy. The word 'cryogenecists' (a made-up-sounding portmanteau) adds to the absurdist texture.

jokes.text: Liz eating Mexican cheese curls at 8am; 'Don't knock my Sabor de Soledad. I found a prize in here the other day... I hope.'
jokes.setup: Jack points out Liz is eating cheese curls at 8am; Liz defends her snack choice.
jokes.punchline: 'I found a prize in here the other day... I hope.' — the 'I hope' undermining her confidence about what the prize was.
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon self-aware-but-not-self-improving characterization. The 'I hope' is the key comedic beat — a tiny two-word amendment that implies the prize might have been something horrifying. It's economical and completely in character. Also plants 'Sabor de Soledad' as a running gag payoff later.

jokes.text: Jack's final line before leaving: 'I have to go. It's time for my freedom search.'
jokes.setup: Jack is saying goodbye to Liz as he heads into the government building.
jokes.punchline: 'It's time for my freedom search' — a portentous, self-important non sequitur for what is presumably a security pat-down.
jokes.explanation: Jack's grandiose reframing of a TSA-style security screening as a 'freedom search' is a sharp satirical jab at post-9/11 government doublespeak, delivered with total sincerity. The humor comes entirely from Jack's complete buy-in to the euphemism.

jokes.text: Tracy bursts in: 'Liz Lemon, do these look like wizard nipples to you?'
jokes.setup: Scene cut with no warning to Tracy asking about wizard nipples.
jokes.punchline: The cold, uncontextualized question itself — delivered as though it's an urgent professional matter.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect cold-open joke beat for Tracy Jordan. The question works on every level: it's surreally specific ('wizard nipples' not just 'nipples'), utterly Tracy, and the lack of any setup makes it funnier. Highly quotable. The specificity of 'wizard nipples' elevates this well above random-=funny; it implies a whole mythos (his video game) that gets explained right after. Economy score is exceptional — five words, maximum absurdity.

jokes.text: Liz responds: 'Are the lightning bolts supposed to be going in or out?'
jokes.setup: Tracy has shown Liz what appear to be wizard nipple designs for his porn video game.
jokes.punchline: Liz engages with the question completely practically, as if nipple-lightning-bolt direction is a legitimate design concern.
jokes.explanation: Liz Lemon's superpower as a character is treating absurd situations with pragmatic professionalism. Her follow-up question perfectly plays the straight man while also revealing she's actually looked at the image and considered it carefully. The 'in or out' specificity is what sells it.

jokes.text: Tracy's porn video game title: 'Goregasm... colon... The Legend of Dong-Slayer'
jokes.setup: Liz asks if the designs are for Tracy's porn video game.
jokes.punchline: The full title: 'Goregasm: The Legend of Dong-Slayer' — delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The title is a masterwork of absurdist naming: 'Goregasm' is a portmanteau that implies violence and sex simultaneously; the epic fantasy subtitle 'The Legend of Dong-Slayer' parodies video game naming conventions (Legend of Zelda) while being lewdly literal. Tracy saying the word 'colon' (the punctuation) adds an extra beat of unintentional anatomical humor. The whole construction is genuinely inspired.

jokes.text: Tracy to Liz: 'Yeah, you fixulate this!' — then immediately apologizing
jokes.setup: Tracy is angry and about to make an obscene gesture at the Korean animators via Liz.
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, you fixulate this!' — a mangled non-word replacing what was clearly supposed to be an obscene phrase, immediately followed by an apology.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's malapropism/neologism 'fixulate' (presumably a garbled version of something obscene) is a character-consistent joke — Tracy frequently invents words. The quick apology pivot is a nice rhythm beat. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Tracy accuses everyone of 'goofing off like a bunch of goof-offs' while standing in the middle of his porn video game production
jokes.setup: Tracy, surrounded by his own absurd professional project, asks Liz if she knows what it's like to be the only one who cares about their job.
jokes.punchline: The irony of Tracy delivering this self-righteous speech about professionalism while filming 'Goregasm: The Legend of Dong-Slayer'.
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is solid — Tracy's complete lack of self-awareness is a core character trait, and the show mines it consistently well. The tautological phrasing 'goof-offs like a bunch of goof-offs' is a small Tracy-specific verbal tick that adds texture.

jokes.text: Tracy asks Liz 'You having your woman times?' — Liz starts to deny it, then realizes she's late
jokes.setup: Liz is emotional; Tracy asks if she's having 'her woman times.'
jokes.punchline: Liz starts to deny it confidently, then trails off as she counts back the weeks and realizes she might be pregnant.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured misdirect that simultaneously plants the episode's main B-plot. Liz's 'Oh, boy' as she trails off is a perfectly timed reaction beat. The phrase 'woman times' is characteristically Tracy — crude but somehow more innocent-sounding than the clinical alternative.

jokes.text: Visual gag: Liz staring at a birth control pill calendar with days crossed off like a prisoner counting days
jokes.setup: Liz has just realized she might be late on her period and is checking her birth control pills.
jokes.punchline: Liz's thought: 'Why don't I cross off the days like people in the movies?' — implying her pill-taking has been inconsistent enough that she can't tell from the pack.
jokes.explanation: A quick confessional-style beat where the joke is Liz's complete chaos around something that should be routine. The movie-reference framing ('like people in the movies') is a gentle meta touch. The humor is more observational-relatable than purely comedic-genius.

jokes.text: Cerie's unsolicited birth control advice: 'I think you're supposed to take all of them, like, in a row.'
jokes.setup: Liz is looking at a scattered mess of birth control pills.
jokes.punchline: Cerie, the beautiful airhead, offers the most basic possible advice as if it's a revelation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — Cerie's one line communicates her character completely (she knows just enough to be useless) while also highlighting how badly Liz is managing her life. 'Like, in a row' is the specific Cerie verbal fingerprint. Very tight.

jokes.text: Liz's comeback to Cerie: 'But I have been sexually active since I was 25.'
jokes.setup: Cerie advises Liz to take her birth control pills in a row.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defensive non-sequitur that she's been sexually active since 25 — an age that is both defensively late and delivered with complete dignity.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. The joke works on three levels: (1) Liz is defending her competence at a task she's clearly failing at, (2) the age of 25 is presented as an achievement rather than a late start, and (3) it completely dodges Cerie's actual point. This is quintessential Liz Lemon — defensive, self-deprecating without intending to be, and oddly dignified. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Pete's memory of Carter's Olympic boycott announced as 'Bad news, archers.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Pete if he ever wanted to go to the Olympics; Pete says he almost went once.
jokes.punchline: Pete's dramatic flashback: 'Bad news, archers. President Carter has decided to boycott the Moscow Games.' — apparently Pete was an Olympic-hopeful archer in 1980.
jokes.explanation: A great Pete joke — Pete's life is a series of near-misses and quiet disappointments, and this backstory fits perfectly. 'Bad news, archers' is a delightful specific detail (Pete was apparently an archer, not a runner or swimmer). The historical specificity of the 1980 Moscow boycott makes it feel earned rather than invented.

jokes.text: Pete's bitter aside after the boycott memory: 'Peanut farmer.'
jokes.setup: Pete has just recalled the Carter Olympic boycott destroying his dreams.
jokes.punchline: A single word, 'Peanut farmer' — Pete's compressed resentment for Carter delivered decades later.
jokes.explanation: Two words of maximum economy. The joke is entirely in the specificity of the insult — not 'Carter' or 'that idiot president' but 'peanut farmer,' Pete's private reduction of a president to his most dismissible trait. The decades of suppressed bitterness compressed into a whispered epithet is Pete's character in miniature. Economy score of 10 is warranted — this is functionally the most compressed joke in the episode.

jokes.text: Donny emerges from hiding in a narrow space waiting to taunt Kenneth
jokes.setup: Kenneth is worried about his Olympic application; Donny appears from an unexpected location.
jokes.punchline: 'I thought you'd be coming out of that door' — Donny was apparently lurking in an alternate location to taunt Kenneth.
jokes.explanation: The joke is mostly physical/visual — Donny has been waiting in an alternate spot just to maximally antagonize Kenneth — but the transcript doesn't give us the full visual payoff. Solid running-gag setup but execution is mid.

jokes.text: Kenneth accuses Donny of sending a false memo about the deadline: 'Saboteur!'
jokes.setup: Kenneth discovers the Olympic application is due today, not in two weeks as his memo stated.
jokes.punchline: 'Saboteur!' — Kenneth's dramatic, slightly archaic accusation.
jokes.explanation: The word choice 'Saboteur!' is perfectly Kenneth — earnest, slightly antiquated, 100% committed. It's funnier than 'You lied!' or 'You cheated!' because it elevates petty workplace rivalry to a wartime crime. Good economy.

jokes.text: Donny gloats: 'You'll be staying here in New York all summer, fighting the crowds, smelling the hot garbage, while I travel to beautiful, breezy Beijing.'
jokes.setup: Donny has successfully sabotaged Kenneth's application timeline.
jokes.punchline: Donny's triumphant tourism-brochure description of Beijing versus the grim New York summer — delivered as pure villain monologue.
jokes.explanation: Functional antagonist gloating. The specific contrast ('hot garbage' vs 'beautiful, breezy Beijing') adds some texture but the joke is fairly conventional. 'Beautiful, breezy Beijing' has some alliterative charm.

jokes.text: Cooter Berger introduces himself: 'vice chair of Farm Subsidies, acting head of FEMA, temporary acting head of the FBC while the acting head is on trial.'
jokes.setup: Jack meets his new government colleague for the first time.
jokes.punchline: The cascade of 'acting' and 'temporary acting' titles ending with 'while the acting head is on trial' — implying constant turnover due to criminal proceedings.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed escalation joke: each title is slightly more provisional than the last, culminating in 'while the acting head is on trial' which recontextualizes all of them as chaos management. The show's political satire is sharp here without being preachy.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I don't like to think of this President as a lame duck. I think of him as a lame eagle.'
jokes.setup: Cooter says it's an exciting time despite the President being a lame duck.
jokes.punchline: 'I think of him as a lame eagle' — correcting the metaphor to a more patriotic but equally damning animal.
jokes.explanation: One of the best political jokes in the episode. The substitution of 'eagle' for 'duck' is brilliant because: (1) it's more patriotic, (2) it doesn't change the fundamental judgment ('lame'), (3) Jack's framing it as a positive rebranding is pure Jack Donaghy spin-doctoring in miniature. Highly quotable, excellent economy, completely in character for someone who reframes disasters as opportunities.

jokes.text: The ceiling is visibly leaking; Cooter insists 'No, it's not. We've looked into it, and it's not.'
jokes.setup: Jack observes the ceiling is leaking.
jokes.punchline: Cooter flatly denies it despite the evidence, because an official government study said it wasn't.
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire about evidence-denying bureaucracy. Cooter's utter sincerity — 'We've looked into it' — is what makes it work. It lands as both a specific political joke (Katrina/FEMA incompetence is clearly referenced) and a universal bureaucracy joke.

jokes.text: No pens in the government office — Cooter has 'gotten used to it' and writes his extension number in the leaking ceiling water
jokes.setup: Cooter offers to write down his extension for Jack.
jokes.punchline: There are no pens in the office; Cooter has adapted to using the ceiling leak water to write — he's gotten so used to it he doesn't even think it's strange.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that rewards the viewer for paying attention. 'I've kind of gotten used to it' is the punchline — the horror of a government official so desensitized to dysfunction that writing with leak water is just a workaround. Sets up the pen running gag.

jokes.text: 'We're not in a recession.' — delivered in response to being asked why there are no pens
jokes.setup: Jack asks why there are no pens.
jokes.punchline: 'We're not in a recession.' — a complete non-answer that implies that acknowledging the pen shortage would be admitting recession.
jokes.explanation: Four words that encapsulate an entire political satire. The logic (buying pens = admitting recession) is both absurd and painfully recognizable. Exceptional economy — you don't need any more words. Cooter's complete seriousness makes it land perfectly. One of the sharpest political jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: 'I know, I'm not drunk either, but we'll manage.' — re: not being prepared for the Appropriations Committee meeting
jokes.setup: Staff member says there's a meeting with the Appropriations Committee; Cooter says he's not prepared.
jokes.punchline: 'I know, I'm not drunk either, but we'll manage.' — implying that being drunk is his standard preparation for congressional meetings.
jokes.explanation: Efficient and dark. The construction is elegant: the staffer's 'I'm not prepared' parallels with Cooter's 'I'm not drunk either' suggesting both are equally necessary prerequisites. It also builds Cooter as a character quickly — he's a man who has fully adapted to dysfunction.

jokes.text: Liz enters Jack's old GE office and starts talking to his mother's portrait, then catches herself
jokes.setup: Liz is lost without Jack and wanders to his old office.
jokes.punchline: She begins asking the portrait of Jack's mother to be her sounding board, then stops herself: 'You're busy. I'll come back another time.'
jokes.explanation: Beautifully pathetic Liz moment. 'I'll come back another time' — she decides to be polite about interrupting a painted portrait. The joke works because she's partially self-aware (she knows Jack isn't there) but still slides into the behavior anyway. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Tracy directing the voice acting session: 'Warrior, you have defeated the snake-elf. Now join me in the orgy chamber. The poets will sing of this night.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is recording voice acting for his porn video game.
jokes.punchline: The earnest epic-fantasy framing of a porn scenario — 'orgy chamber,' 'the poets will sing of this night' — Tracy's complete commitment to the mythology of his game.
jokes.explanation: 'The poets will sing of this night' is a legitimately inspired phrase for a porn game scenario. Tracy treating the Dong-Slayer universe with epic-fantasy gravitas is consistently funny throughout, and this moment is a peak example. The 'snake-elf' is a specific absurd detail that implies a whole elaborate world.

jokes.text: Tracy to Jenna after stopping the session: 'Not you, Grizz. You're doing great.' while firing Jenna for bad acting
jokes.setup: Tracy stops the recording, frustrated. Everyone thinks they're being criticized.
jokes.punchline: 'Not you, Grizz. You're doing great.' — Grizz (a large man who memorized his lines) is the star performer; Jenna the professional actress is the problem.
jokes.explanation: The inversion — Grizz (the non-actor) outperforming Jenna (the professional) in a porn video game — is perfectly executed. The specificity of 'I memorized all my lines at home' from Grizz makes it funnier: he prepared like a real professional. Economy is excellent. This is a strong joke.

jokes.text: Tracy's avatar sensuality direction sequence: 'Touch my cheek... chest area... little robot... butt... like it's a secret... knees-butt... feet with your knees'
jokes.setup: Tracy is listing player sensuality options for the video game avatars.
jokes.punchline: The escalating weirdness of the sensuality map — ending with 'knees-butt' (a new body part) and 'feet with your knees' — a sequence that starts normal and ends in pure anatomical absurdism.
jokes.explanation: A masterfully escalating joke sequence. Starts with recognizable body parts (cheek, chest), adds a dance move ('little robot'), goes normal again (butt), adds a modifier ('like it's a secret' — why?!), then invents an entirely new body part ('knees-butt'), and finally achieves full anatomical incoherence ('feet with your knees'). The structure is perfect escalation comedy — each step is slightly more absurd than the last, and 'knees-butt' is a genuine comedic invention. One of the strongest joke sequences in the episode.

jokes.text: Tracy directing Jenna's sex sounds, then calling 'Let's take it again from the top. This time, let's record.' — revealing they weren't recording
jokes.setup: Tracy has been directing an extended session of sex sounds from Jenna, including 'Wonderful, wonderful.'
jokes.punchline: 'This time, let's record.' — the entire elaborate session was a rehearsal; Tracy wasn't even recording.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection structure. The scene builds expectation that this is a recording session; the punchline is that Jenna just performed all of that for nothing, and Tracy (the director) was satisfied enough to want to do it again. The 'Wonderful, wonderful' preceding it makes the reveal land harder — he was this satisfied with an uncaptured rehearsal. Strong structural joke.

jokes.text: Liz's voicemail to Jack, interrupted by the sex sounds session in progress: 'Aah! Things are happening!'
jokes.setup: Liz is leaving Jack a voicemail about needing his advice, while surrounded by Tracy's recording session.
jokes.punchline: 'Aah! Things are happening!' — Liz's complete collapse of professional composure as she's startled by Tracy's direction.
jokes.explanation: A funny reaction beat — Liz trying to maintain a calm professional voicemail tone while surrounded by chaos is a recurring 30 Rock pleasure. 'Things are happening!' as a summary of everything wrong is endearingly vague.

jokes.text: Government official refuses $9 million dam funding: ''Dam' is a swear word.' Proposes calling it a 'God finger' instead.
jokes.setup: The Appropriations Committee is discussing Portland's dam system request.
jokes.punchline: A committee member vetoes it because 'dam' is a swear word, then proposes the sexually suggestive 'God finger' as the alternative.
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly constructed two-part joke: the first part (prudishness about 'dam') satirizes the religious-right bowdlerization of language; the second part (proposing 'God finger,' which is sexually explicit) demonstrates complete obliviousness. The extra beat 'Randall, must you bring religion into everything?' misreads the situation in a third funny way. Three comedy layers in two sentences. Strong.

jokes.text: Jack's speech to the committee about pens escalates to 'We need hope. We need change. We need experience. We need pens.'
jokes.setup: Jack is making an impassioned speech about American potential to the Appropriations Committee.
jokes.punchline: After invoking 'hope,' 'change,' and 'experience' — the actual 2008 campaign buzzwords — the final item on the list is 'pens.'
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured callback that also functions as political satire. Jack co-opts the actual 2008 campaign slogans (Obama's 'hope and change,' Clinton's 'experience') and deflates the entire rhetorical tradition with 'We need pens.' The structural decision to put 'pens' last — after the high-minded abstractions — is textbook comedy rhythm. The callback to the pen shortage makes it doubly funny. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Committee member response to Jack's Rome speech: 'Well, that's one theory.'
jokes.setup: Jack says 'Rome wasn't built in a day.'
jokes.punchline: 'Well, that's one theory.' — treating a common idiom as a contestable historical hypothesis.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully timed background-character deadpan. The joke is that an obvious platitude is treated with the skepticism of a peer-reviewed paper. Economy is nearly perfect — four words do a lot of work. Character integration is low because this is a one-off background character, but the line itself is excellent.

jokes.text: Kenneth explains his lateness: 'I had to put on my jeans by myself.'
jokes.setup: Jenna asks where Kenneth has been.
jokes.punchline: 'I had to put on my jeans by myself.' — implying either that Kenneth normally needs help with this, or that it was unusually difficult for some reason.
jokes.explanation: A very Kenneth line — the apology itself implies a strange domestic reality that the show never explains. The joke is entirely in the gap between what was said and what it implies. Economy is exceptional: eight words suggest an entire absurd lifestyle.

jokes.text: Donny emerges from Jenna's bag: 'Did someone say 'Donny'? No. No. Oh. It's pretty muffled in there.'
jokes.setup: No one said 'Donny'; Donny has been hiding inside Jenna's bag to eavesdrop.
jokes.punchline: Donny crawls out of a bag he's been hiding in, explaining 'It's pretty muffled in there' — acknowledging he misheard because he was secreted inside a bag.
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag — the audience sees Donny emerge from an impossibly small bag. 'It's pretty muffled in there' is the perfect explanation: he confirms the absurd situation with practical detail, as if hiding in bags is a normal strategy. The triple 'No. No.' from the room before his excuse is well-timed.

jokes.text: Liz explaining 'back-door brag': 'It's hard for me to watch American Idol because I have perfect pitch.'
jokes.setup: Liz is teaching Kenneth how to brag about himself indirectly.
jokes.punchline: Her demonstration perfectly illustrates the back-door brag — sandwiching a boast inside a complaint — and is also self-deprecating about the kind of person who does this.
jokes.explanation: The 'back-door brag' concept itself is an original comedic construction (though the phrase predates 30 Rock). The example given is perfectly crafted: the complaint is genuine, the boast is specific and obnoxious. It also works as character comedy for Liz — she knows exactly how insufferable this is and does it anyway. Highly quotable, the concept is memorable.

jokes.text: Kenneth's attempt at a back-door brag: 'It's hard for me to watch American Idol because there's a water bug on my channel changer.'
jokes.setup: Liz has taught Kenneth about the back-door brag; Kenneth tries one.
jokes.punchline: Instead of bragging about himself, Kenneth's 'brag' reveals only a household pest problem — his version has no brag at all.
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect joke. The structure is immaculate: parallel construction of Liz's example, but with the brag replaced by mundane rural misery. The joke reveals Kenneth's humility, poverty, and guilelessness simultaneously. He has no achievements to brag about — or he genuinely doesn't think his qualities are brag-worthy. The specific detail 'water bug on my channel changer' is funnier than any generic alternative could be. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Cooter: 'I haven't felt this energized at work since the two weeks when they tried to teach us Farsi.'
jokes.setup: Cooter is telling Jack how happy he is to have him there.
jokes.punchline: His most recent point of comparison for workplace energy is a failed two-week Farsi training — implying both the randomness of administration priorities and the two-week lifespan of any initiative.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'two weeks' and 'Farsi' does heavy lifting. Farsi implies post-9/11 military-intelligence priorities; 'two weeks' suggests the administration's characteristic inability to follow through on anything. The joke paints Cooter's whole working life in one sentence.

jokes.text: Jack hears that Geiss spoke from his coma and said 'Jackie Boy' — and immediately writes his resignation letter
jokes.setup: Geiss, who has been in a coma, apparently spoke — Jack was just told this.
jokes.punchline: The single phrase 'Jackie Boy' — Jack's nickname — is enough for Jack to immediately resign from government service, treating a coma patient's mumble as a definitive succession announcement.
jokes.explanation: Jack's single-mindedness about the GE CEO position is core character comedy. The absurdity of treating a barely-conscious coma patient's utterance as legally binding corporate succession is perfect. The speed of the reaction (immediate resignation) is the joke — Jack needs almost no evidence.

jokes.text: Cooter refuses to accept Jack's resignation because as acting head of the FBC he oversees the EWPC
jokes.setup: Jack tries to resign; Cooter says he can deny the resignation.
jokes.punchline: Cooter invokes an acronym cascade — FBC, EWPC — to legally trap Jack in government service, bureaucracy weaponized against an individual.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the absurdity of government acronyms being used as prison bars. Functional political satire but the acronyms themselves aren't meaningful enough to be extra funny — they're just gibberish with plausible structure.

jokes.text: Jack's final appeal to Cooter invokes GE's slogan: 'He brings good things to light!'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to convince Cooter to let him leave government to run GE.
jokes.punchline: Jack quotes GE's actual advertising slogan 'He brings good things to light' with total sincerity as the capstone of his argument — the show (produced by NBC/Universal, a GE company) referencing its parent company's slogan.
jokes.explanation: Meta-referential humor: 30 Rock is on NBC, owned by GE, and Jack is a GE executive. Using the actual GE slogan as a sincere rhetorical flourish is a layered joke about the show's own corporate ownership. Works on multiple levels for attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Cooter's resignation pile: 'Look at these resignation letters. They're written in ketchup, dirty rock, leak water.'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to convince Cooter that the government job is destroying them both.
jokes.punchline: Cooter reveals a stack of resignation letters written in improvised materials because there were no pens — ketchup, a dirty rock, and the leak water.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant callback that pays off two running gags simultaneously (no pens + the leak) while creating a viscerally funny image. 'Dirty rock' is the standout word choice — the specificity of 'dirty' makes it funnier than just 'rock.' The image of someone scratching 'RESIGNATION' into paper with a dirty rock in desperation is both comic and genuinely pathetic. This is excellent comedy writing.

jokes.text: Liz figures out her friend is pregnant: 'You're pregnant.' 'What? Yes! How can you tell?' 'I just can. People always underestimate my instincts because of my looks.'
jokes.setup: Liz encounters her friend and immediately announces she's pregnant.
jokes.punchline: 'People always underestimate my instincts because of my looks.' — a back-door brag about appearance that is itself a back-door brag, immediately called out.
jokes.explanation: A lovely callback to the back-door brag concept — the friend inadvertently does a back-door brag right after the concept was introduced, which Liz (and the audience) immediately recognizes. 'This is no time for back-door bragging!' is a funny follow-up. Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Liz: 'It is Floyd, right?' — implying doubt about who the father is
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to comfort her friend about the pregnancy and suggests she call Floyd.
jokes.punchline: Liz's aside '...Oh, no. It is Floyd, right?' — a beat of dawning horror that the friend might not know.
jokes.explanation: The comedic beat is in the pause — the moment where Liz realizes she maybe shouldn't have assumed. The margaritas cutaway that follows as a quick flashback is the implied answer. Good timing joke.

jokes.text: Cutaway to margarita night: 'Whoo! Those margaritas were strong.'
jokes.setup: Liz has asked if Floyd is the father with some doubt; the answer is provided via flashback.
jokes.punchline: A brief flashback to a margarita night suggests the paternity is unclear — 'Those margaritas were strong' as an explanation/excuse.
jokes.explanation: Quick cutaway gag in classic 30 Rock style. The line itself is economical and does the job but doesn't add much beyond confirming what was implied.

jokes.text: Liz discovers her friend slept with Dennis: 'It was before he tried to throw me under the subway train.'
jokes.setup: Liz is horrified to learn her friend slept with Dennis.
jokes.punchline: The friend's defense: it was before Dennis tried to throw her under a subway train — implying that was where she drew the line, not before.
jokes.explanation: A very funny character-dark joke. The implication is that attempted subway murder is a reasonable breakup point but apparently not a dealbreaker before it happens. Dennis's villainy is conveyed efficiently and humorously. The matter-of-fact delivery amplifies the absurdity.

jokes.text: Liz's response: 'You had a three-way with Roseanne and Tom Arnold.'
jokes.setup: Friend accuses Liz of being the only one allowed to make sex mistakes.
jokes.punchline: Liz's comeback invokes a real-celebrity three-way as her equivalent 'sex mistake.'
jokes.explanation: The specific celebrity choice of Roseanne and Tom Arnold is inspired — they're a real former couple, which makes the scenario more vivid and specific. The joke works because the choice of celebrities is both surprising and weirdly specific. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Liz's single-mom role models: 'Like Erin Brockovich or Sarah Connor.'
jokes.setup: Liz says she'll be a kick-ass single mom.
jokes.punchline: Her examples: Erin Brockovich (a legal activist) and Sarah Connor (a fictional character fighting machines from the future) — presented as equivalent.
jokes.explanation: The pairing of a real person with a fictional action hero as equivalent single-mom role models is a classic 30 Rock joke structure. It's character-specific for Liz (she'd reference both pop culture and actual people without distinguishing between them). The absurdist logic is earned.

jokes.text: Liz's advice to her friend: 'And while you're there, try to get me some Adderall.'
jokes.setup: Liz advises her friend to go get a blood test to confirm the pregnancy.
jokes.punchline: 'And while you're there, try to get me some Adderall.' — tacked onto genuine advice, Liz uses the doctor's visit for her own pharmaceutical needs.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — 10 words attached to caring advice completely undermine it. The pivot from supportive friend to 'also get me drugs' is a great Liz beat. Fully character-integrated: Liz is simultaneously caring and completely self-centered.

jokes.text: Cooter, upon pens arriving: 'We've got pens! Glorious pens!'
jokes.setup: Pens have finally arrived at the government office
jokes.punchline: 'Glorious pens!' — the celebration is disproportionate to the achievement, but given everything we know about Cooter's situation, it's also heartbreaking
jokes.explanation: The pen running gag is delivered with genuine emotion here. 'Glorious pens' is a perfect reaction — the word 'glorious' for office supplies is both absurd and sad given Cooter's context.

jokes.text: The pens arrive — but they're all caps: 'Oh, my God! They're caps, nothing but caps!'
jokes.setup: Pens have finally arrived after the whole episode's buildup.
jokes.punchline: The pens have no ink cartridges — just caps — a new level of Kafkaesque government failure.
jokes.explanation: A textbook escalation payoff. The entire episode builds toward pens arriving; the subversion is that the pens are defective in the most specific, pathetic possible way — caps only. The image of a man opening a pen box to find nothing but plastic caps is a perfect visual joke. The structure earns maximum points: the longer the setup, the funnier the underwhelming payoff. One of the episode's best payoffs.

jokes.text: Cooter breaks down: 'That's not my name! My name is James Reilly! Cooter Berger? What do you think I am, a cartoon dog?'
jokes.setup: Jack has just called him 'Cooter' again after the caps disaster.
jokes.punchline: 'What do you think I am, a cartoon dog?' — Cooter's legitimate complaint that his nickname sounds absurd, paired with the specific comparison to cartoon dogs.
jokes.explanation: The breakdown is earned by the caps payoff, and 'What do you think I am, a cartoon dog?' is genuinely inspired — it's the kind of thing you'd only think to say if you'd been living with a terrible nickname for years. The follow-through (explaining the origin of both 'Cooter' AND 'Berger') makes it even better.

jokes.text: Origin of 'Cooter Berger': 'Cooter because I look like a turtle, and Berger because he saw me eating a hamburger one time.' — 'It wasn't even a hamburger. It was a sandwich.'
jokes.setup: Cooter explains how the President gave him both nicknames.
jokes.punchline: 'It wasn't even a hamburger. It was a sandwich.' — the final indignity is that the naming event wasn't even accurate.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best in 30 Rock's run. Structure is immaculate: (1) 'Cooter' because he looks like a turtle — already absurd and demeaning; (2) 'Berger' because the President saw him eating a hamburger — absurd basis for a nickname; (3) delivered separately after a beat: 'It wasn't even a hamburger. It was a sandwich.' — the final coda that recontextualizes the entire name and adds a third layer of pathetic detail. The pause before the sandwich reveal is everything. This is comparable to the Snip-snap vasectomy calibration example in structure and character-pathos comedy. Genuinely exceptional.

jokes.text: Jack's plan to get fired: 'We have to work together to get fired.'
jokes.setup: They can't resign; Jack proposes the only alternative.
jokes.punchline: The inverted logic — two ambitious men conspiring not to achieve but to be fired — as the only path to freedom.
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the next act. The absurdity of the plan is good (proud men scheming to be fired) but it's more of a premise statement than a fully executed joke.

jokes.text: Cooter's addendum: 'It wasn't even a hamburger. It was a sandwich.'
jokes.setup: Cooter has just explained that his nickname 'Berger' came from the President seeing him eat a hamburger
jokes.punchline: Clarifying that it was actually a sandwich — the nickname was based on a factual error — and this detail is apparently important to him
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The callback detail 'it wasn't even a hamburger, it was a sandwich' lands as a perfect button — the entire name is based on a misidentification. The timing (delivered after the scene has seemingly moved on) and the economy (ten words) are exceptional. It implies Cooter has been silently correcting this fact in his head for years while accepting the nickname. This is the kind of joke that makes a room erupt. Justifies high score.

jokes.text: Dennis has been sneaking into Liz's apartment to pretend to be at work: 'I told my mom I got a job, so I've been coming here for the past couple weeks during the day.'
jokes.setup: Liz finds Dennis in her apartment; he explains why.
jokes.punchline: Dennis has been using Liz's apartment as a fake workplace to deceive his mother, despite having no relationship with Liz.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Dennis. The layered awfulness here: (1) he's still treating Liz's apartment as accessible to him; (2) he's lying to his mother about employment; (3) the solution was to fake-work at his ex's apartment. Fully character-integrated — this is exactly the kind of pathetic detail that makes Dennis a great comedic villain.

jokes.text: Dennis's definition of 'prenatal': 'Pre... before. Natal... ruined.'
jokes.setup: Dennis sees Liz's prenatal vitamins and says he knows what 'prenatal' means.
jokes.punchline: 'Pre... before. Natal... ruined.' — Dennis's genuine attempt at etymology produces a definition that reveals his attitude toward fatherhood.
jokes.explanation: This is the best single joke in the episode and one of the finest wordplay/character jokes in 30 Rock's run. The structure is perfect: Dennis attempts to demonstrate intelligence by breaking down the Latin, gets 'pre' right (barely), then delivers 'natal... ruined' — which is both wrong as etymology AND perfectly characterizes Dennis's view of children and his own life. It's a triple-decker joke: it's funny as wordplay, funnier as character revelation, and funniest as a commentary on Dennis's entire life philosophy. Maximum economy. Completely original. Utterly character-specific. This clears the 9.5 calibration bar.

jokes.text: Dennis names his unborn son 'Morpheus': 'If it's a boy, we're gonna name him Morpheus, like that guy in The Matrix.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is planning names for the baby.
jokes.punchline: 'Morpheus, like that guy in The Matrix.' — the clarification 'like that guy in The Matrix' suggests Dennis thinks Morpheus needs identification, and the Matrix version is the only Morpheus he knows.
jokes.explanation: The clarification 'like that guy in The Matrix' is the punchline — it reveals Dennis has no awareness of Morpheus as a classical name, and also that he considers The Matrix a sufficient cultural touchstone for naming a child. Character-perfect.

jokes.text: Dennis's exit line: 'Morpheus hears everything that you say.' then 'Your boobs are gonna get bigger.'
jokes.setup: Liz is throwing Dennis out.
jokes.punchline: Dennis invokes fetal sentience to shame Liz ('Morpheus hears everything') then follows up with a leering comment about her body as his parting shot.
jokes.explanation: Two-part exit joke that's perfectly calibrated: the first part ('Morpheus hears everything') is pompous fatherhood theater; the second ('your boobs are gonna get bigger') demolishes any dignity he'd just constructed and reveals his actual priorities. The pivot is fast and devastating. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dennis's parting shot: 'Your boobs are gonna get bigger.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just thrown Dennis out
jokes.punchline: Dennis's final comment as he leaves — treating Liz's body as something relevant to his interests even as he's being ejected
jokes.explanation: Pure Dennis — using a leaving moment to make it about Liz's body. Economy is excellent (five words). Character-perfect but not highly original.

jokes.text: Jenna's opening of Kenneth's essay, talking to camera about herself: 'You must have been such a pretty monkey.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has written Kenneth's personal essay as if she is writing about him.
jokes.punchline: Her essay begins with a compliment she would give herself — 'You must have been such a pretty monkey' — suggesting she is either describing herself or her odd conception of Kenneth.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant character joke — Jenna writing 'you must have been such a pretty monkey' as the opening of someone else's personal essay reveals that she can only process another person through the lens of her own narcissism. The specific phrase 'pretty monkey' is wonderfully strange — it's simultaneously a genuine (if bizarre) compliment and a complete failure to write about Kenneth. One of the episode's best character-specific jokes.

jokes.text: Jenna's fake talking-head promoting Kenneth includes: 'Yes. Kenneth, can you take this money to the many charities I support anonymously?' — then the envelope is empty
jokes.setup: Jenna is recording a fake documentary talking-head about Kenneth's charity work.
jokes.punchline: She gives Kenneth an envelope for 'the many charities I support anonymously' — but when Kenneth opens it, it's empty. The charity is entirely performative.
jokes.explanation: The empty charity envelope is a great visual gag that perfectly captures Jenna's character: she wants credit for generosity without the inconvenience of actual generosity. The 'anonymously' is the key word — she supports charities anonymously except when she can mention it in video essays.

jokes.text: Jenna's essay claims Kenneth 'can lift almost 100 pounds' as a fitness achievement
jokes.setup: Jenna is trying to portray Kenneth's physical fitness.
jokes.punchline: 'He can lift almost 100 pounds!' — presented as an impressive athletic feat; 100 lbs is a modest weight for a grown man.
jokes.explanation: A solid understated joke — 'almost 100 pounds' is the damning qualifier. The joke is that Jenna thinks this is impressive, revealing both her ignorance of fitness and her low opinion of Kenneth.

jokes.text: Jenna's essay fragments: 'Mind, body, spirit? / Kenneth, I see myself in you? / So brave? / So ready? / To be all that you can do? / So beautiful in every way? / I see myself in you?'
jokes.setup: Jenna continues her 'essay' for Kenneth.
jokes.punchline: Every statement is a question (rising intonation/uncertainty), the army slogan is garbled ('all that you can do' vs 'be all that you can be'), and 'I see myself in you' repeats — it's a personal essay entirely about Jenna.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Jenna's essay being entirely about herself reaches its peak here. The question marks on everything (uncertainty even in her praise), the misquoted Army slogan, and the repeated 'I see myself in you' all build to the joke that Jenna has written a personal essay for someone else that is entirely about Jenna. The repetition of 'I see myself in you' is the clincher — she's not even pretending anymore.

jokes.text: Jenna's essay ends with the line 'To be all that you can do?' — mangling the Army's slogan
jokes.setup: Jenna is trying to use motivational language in her essay-video
jokes.punchline: 'To be all that you can do' — mixing up 'be all that you can be' (Army) and 'just do it' (Nike) into a meaningless hybrid
jokes.explanation: The slogan mashup is a nice detail that reveals Jenna's superficial relationship with language and inspiration. Subtle enough to reward attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Jenna, having been moved by her own speech, calls after Kenneth about copier paper as he runs out: 'Oh, Kenneth, someone was looking for you. They need 12 boxes of copier paper on stage one.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been inspired by Jenna's speech and is rushing to submit his application.
jokes.punchline: Jenna, who has been doing all this for Kenneth, casually passes along a menial errand request that will derail him — completely oblivious to the obstacle she's just placed.
jokes.explanation: Great character beat — Jenna's complete lack of awareness that the menial task will undermine everything she just did. The timing (right as Kenneth is running out inspired) makes it funnier. Sets up Kenneth's physical comedy sequence.

jokes.text: Someone asks Kenneth to move 12 boxes of copier paper on stage right after he's about to run to submit his application
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been inspired and has 20 minutes to submit his application
jokes.punchline: He's immediately derailed by a mundane page task — 12 boxes of copier paper — the universe conspiring against him
jokes.explanation: Functional obstacle comedy. The specificity of '12 boxes' adds some texture but this is primarily a plot beat rather than a great joke.

jokes.text: The gay bomb: Jack and Cooter's plan to get fired involves a Pentagon 1994 proposal for a weapon that would 'make enemy soldiers totally gaybones for each other'
jokes.setup: Jack and Cooter are brainstorming something 'wasteful, embarrassing, and upsetting to voters' to get themselves fired.
jokes.punchline: The 'gay bomb' — a real(ish) Pentagon proposal described with the invented term 'gaybones' — is their chosen vehicle.
jokes.explanation: The 'gay bomb' is based on a real 1994 Pentagon proposal, which gives it a satirical grounding. 'Totally gaybones' is an inventive and funny coinage. The joke works as political satire and absurdist comedy simultaneously.

jokes.text: Re: why the gay bomb project was abandoned: 'It would have been expensive, impractical, and offensive to both the red states and the gayer blue states.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Cooter are reviewing why the original project was cancelled.
jokes.punchline: '...offensive to both the red states and the gayer blue states.' — 'the gayer blue states' is a brilliant political characterization that acknowledges gay demographics while being gently satirical.
jokes.explanation: 'The gayer blue states' is a phrase that packs surprising political observation into three words. It acknowledges LGBT demographics as a voting constituency while gently satirizing the blue-state political coalition. Smart, economical, and funny.

jokes.text: Jack's aside: 'Like eating a burrito before sex.'
jokes.setup: Jack is describing their gay bomb plan as 'a guaranteed disaster.'
jokes.punchline: 'Like eating a burrito before sex.' — an unasked-for personal comparison that implies Jack has this specific experience.
jokes.explanation: An odd, specific, funny aside from Jack that implies a rich personal history with poor decision-making. The specificity ('burrito' not just 'Mexican food') is what makes it funny. A quick joke that lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Frank's credit on the porn video game: 'I got an Additional Filth By credit.'
jokes.setup: Tracy reveals the Dong-Slayer game to Frank as a prototype.
jokes.punchline: 'Additional Filth By' — a parody film/TV credit applied to a porn video game, implying there was already filth that Frank merely added to.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully conceived. The parody of film credits ('Additional Dialogue By,' 'Additional Photography By') applied to pornographic content is precise and funny. 'Additional Filth By' implies that the base level of filth was established elsewhere and Frank merely contributed supplementary filth. The specific word 'filth' versus any softer alternative is the right choice. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Donny gloats over Kenneth's copier paper task: 'Too bad it cost you a trip to China.' / 'Looks like you only have 30 seconds to get your application to the 27th floor. And you're not gonna make it.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is trying to carry copier paper and submit his application simultaneously.
jokes.punchline: Donny gloats with villainous precision while giving Kenneth a countdown.
jokes.explanation: Functional plot-advancing antagonist dialogue. The joke is really in the situation (Kenneth trying to manage copier paper + deadline) rather than the specific lines. Donny's gloating is repetitive by this point in the episode. Below average for this episode.

jokes.text: Donny reveals the application was for the WRONG person, with 30 seconds left: 'Looks like you only have 30 seconds to get your application to the 27th floor. And you're not gonna make it.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth has just submitted his application with relief
jokes.punchline: The application was submitted for someone else — he has 30 seconds to resubmit on a different floor, which seems impossible
jokes.explanation: Plot mechanics with some comedic energy from the escalation. More plot than joke.

jokes.text: Kenneth's physical comedy sequence: running with copier paper, crashing, doing a flip into an elevator
jokes.setup: Kenneth has 30 seconds to get his application to the 27th floor while carrying 12 boxes of copier paper.
jokes.punchline: Liz's voicemail captures the chaos: 'What? Kenneth just did a flip into the elevator.' — Kenneth apparently performs athletically impossible maneuvers while fully loaded with paper.
jokes.explanation: Excellent physical comedy moment. 'Kenneth just did a flip into the elevator' as a throwaway detail in Liz's panicked voicemail makes it funnier than if it were dramatized — the casualness of the delivery amplifies the absurdity. Kenneth's hidden physical abilities are a running character thing. The impact score reflects the visual comedy value.

jokes.text: Liz's collapsing voicemails to Jack: from casual to 'This is a disaster. This baby's gonna have a father!'
jokes.setup: Liz has been leaving increasingly panicked voicemails for Jack throughout the episode.
jokes.punchline: 'This baby's gonna have a father!' — said with horror, as though a baby having a father is the disaster scenario.
jokes.explanation: A great inverted line. Conventionally, 'the baby's gonna have a father' is good news; Liz treats it as catastrophe because the father is Dennis. The subversion of conventional expectation is sharp and fully character-integrated. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: C.C. to Jack: 'I did certain things for you in bed that you were going to reciprocate. But then we broke up before my birthday, so you owe me.'
jokes.setup: C.C. is explaining why she'll help Jack with the gay bomb despite their breakup.
jokes.punchline: The reason is outstanding sexual reciprocity debt — she performed sexual acts she's owed in return, and the breakup created a non-sexual debt.
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly sophisticated cringe joke. The transactional nature of C.C.'s sexual accounting — she's kept track, there's a debt, she's calling it in for a gay bomb budget appropriation — is both absurd and completely in character for a congressperson who lives and dies by quid pro quo. The bureaucratic framing of intimacy is sharp.

jokes.text: Jack's reaction to C.C. agreeing to help: 'Yes! I am so on a roll! No crying in my bath tonight.'
jokes.setup: C.C. agrees to help get the gay bomb approved.
jokes.punchline: 'No crying in my bath tonight.' — Jack's victory celebration implies he has been crying in his bath on other nights, revealing vulnerability beneath the alpha-male exterior.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Jack jokes in the episode. 'No crying in my bath tonight' is funny on its own as an unexpected confession, but it's also deeply character-specific: Jack Donaghy's emotional vulnerability expressed as a manly bath-cry is perfect. It implies a whole interior life. The economy is superb — the positive statement ('no crying') reveals the negative reality (there has been crying, possibly regularly). Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Compilation of Liz's escalating voicemails to Jack, now including pregnancy and Kenneth's acrobatics
jokes.setup: The show replays/continues Liz's voicemail chain to Jack.
jokes.punchline: Voicemails now include: thinking she's pregnant with Dennis's baby, calling it 'what I wanted,' and reporting Kenneth did a flip into an elevator — all presented with equal urgency.
jokes.explanation: The voicemail gag pays off well here — the juxtaposition of 'I think I'm pregnant with Dennis Duffy's baby. Thought you'd be super proud.' with the complete emotional breakdown immediately after is good escalation. The callback structure rewards viewers who've been tracking the gag.

jokes.text: Liz's extended voicemail about converting her 'laundry and newspaper pile into a nursery'
jokes.setup: Liz has been looking at cribs online and is getting excited about the pregnancy.
jokes.punchline: The 'nursery' will be built in her current 'laundry and newspaper pile' — her apartment is so chaotic that a pile of laundry and newspapers is the designated nursery space.
jokes.explanation: A solid Liz Lemon domestic disaster joke. 'Laundry and newspaper pile' as an existing named household feature suggests she's so accustomed to her own disorder that she treats the pile as permanent furniture. Good character specificity.

jokes.text: The Sabor de Soledad revelation: Mexican cheese curls get their 'special tangy flavor from evaporated bull semen' and were causing false positives on pregnancy tests
jokes.setup: Liz has been eating Sabor de Soledad throughout the episode; the mystery ingredient is finally revealed.
jokes.punchline: The 'special tangy flavor' is evaporated bull semen — the prize in the bag from the opening scene suddenly takes on new meaning.
jokes.explanation: A masterfully constructed long-running payoff. The cheese curls were established as a character quirk in scene one; the 'I found a prize in here' line takes on retroactive horror; the false pregnancy tests are explained by the same ingredient; and Jack's line 'Oh, that explains your hair's thickness and shine' delivers a second joke in the same breath. The payoff is both gross and structurally excellent — everything was setup. This is 30 Rock at its best: jokes planted 20 minutes earlier paying off with maximum impact.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Oh, that explains your hair's thickness and shine.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just been told she's been eating bull semen in her snacks.
jokes.punchline: Jack's first response is not horror but practical observation — the bull semen explains a positive cosmetic effect he's noticed.
jokes.explanation: Arguably the single best delivery beat in the episode. Jack's deadpan pivot to 'that explains your hair's thickness and shine' is perfect for multiple reasons: (1) Jack has been noticing Liz's hair; (2) bull semen as a hair treatment is an actual thing; (3) his matter-of-fact tone suggests he's been puzzling over this for some time. The line is a second complete joke stacked on top of the already-great semen reveal. Extremely quotable, completely Jack.

jokes.text: 'I guess in Mexico women use it to stop their periods before Cinco de Mayo.'
jokes.setup: The bull semen in Sabor de Soledad has been revealed; Jack continues with additional product facts.
jokes.punchline: The chip's use case in Mexico — period suppression before Cinco de Mayo — is presented as matter-of-fact product knowledge Jack somehow has.
jokes.explanation: A triple-stacked joke: (1) the absurd medical use case for the chip; (2) the culturally specific 'Cinco de Mayo' as the occasion worth suppressing your period for; (3) Jack's matter-of-fact delivery suggesting this is in his knowledge base. 'Before Cinco de Mayo' is a perfect specific detail — why that holiday specifically? The show never explains, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I'm a little afraid to ask if you're still eating them.' / Liz: 'They're so good.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just been told the snacks she loves contain evaporated bull semen.
jokes.punchline: 'They're so good.' — Liz continues eating Sabor de Soledad anyway.
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly close the episode's Sabor de Soledad arc. 'They're so good' is Liz Lemon's character in its purest form: knowing something is terrible and choosing it anyway because it brings her pleasure. Jack's hesitant setup ('I'm a little afraid to ask') and Liz's immediate, shameless answer is perfect comedic rhythm. The economy score of 10 is warranted — you cannot say this in fewer words with more impact.

jokes.text: Liz: 'No, I can't go to a sperm bank. The Duffy men use those like ATMs.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks about artificial insemination as an alternative to adoption.
jokes.punchline: 'The Duffy men use those like ATMs.' — implying the Duffy family has so thoroughly saturated sperm banks that Liz risks accidentally using Dennis-adjacent genetic material.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The ATM simile is inspired — it implies regularity, volume, convenience, and a somewhat mercenary relationship to the enterprise. 'The Duffy men' as a plural suggests a whole family tradition of prolific sperm donation that has contaminated the entire bank. Extremely quotable, high originality, maximum economy. This approaches the calibration anchor quality.

jokes.text: Jack reveals the President gave him a nickname too: 'The Jacker.' Both Jack and Liz react with resignation.
jokes.setup: Jack mentions his day casually; Liz asks how it was.
jokes.punchline: 'The President gave me a nickname. The Jacker.' — delivered flatly, as if this is a minor detail.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly executed callback to the Cooter Berger nickname reveal. The President has been established as a random nickname-giver; now Jack gets 'The Jacker' — which has obvious unintended sexual connotations. Jack's flat delivery and Liz's 'Yeah.' suggest they're both aware of the connotations and have moved past them. The economy and callback structure are excellent.

jokes.text: The gay bomb actually works on Jack and Cooter in the committee room — both men start to feel weird
jokes.setup: Jack and Cooter have been trying to get fired using the gay bomb proposal; the actual chemical is apparently deployed.
jokes.punchline: 'I feel weird. Let's do this.' — Jack and Cooter, having inadvertently been exposed to the gay bomb, apparently experience its effects together.
jokes.explanation: The payoff works because 'I feel weird. Let's do this.' is perfectly ambiguous — it could mean they're going forward with the plan to get fired, or it could mean the bomb is working. The double meaning is intentional and well-constructed. The callback to Cooter noting the chemical only works in 'closed, unventilated spaces' (which a committee room is) makes this a well-planted payoff.

jokes.text: Pens follow-up: 'Ooh, pens!' — a committee member reaches for the pen caps in the committee room
jokes.setup: The pen-cap box from earlier apparently ended up in the committee room.
jokes.punchline: 'Ooh, pens!' — exclaimed with delight, someone grabs for them not knowing they're just caps.
jokes.explanation: A nice tag on the pen gag. The exclamation 'Ooh, pens!' mirrors the 'U.S.A.!' moment, and the dramatic irony (we know they're caps) adds a layer. Not a showstopper but a satisfying callback.

jokes.text: Frank has been playing Dong-Slayer for three months without realizing it: 'Dude, I played this thing for a couple hours. It's okay, I guess.' / 'Frank, you've been in your office for three months.'
jokes.setup: Tracy presents the prototype Dong-Slayer game to Frank.
jokes.punchline: Frank thinks he played for 'a couple hours' — it has actually been three months. The game is so consuming he lost three months of his life.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed cold-close joke. The setup is Frank's understatement ('a couple hours, it's okay I guess'); the punchline is the complete scale inversion (three months). Tracy's follow-up 'Yes! I'm gonna be a billionaire!' is the perfect button. The structure mirrors great escalation jokes — you expect a small gap between perception and reality, and get a massive one instead. Strong closer.

jokes.text: Frank has been playing Goregasm for three months and his reaction: 'Yes! I'm gonna be a billionaire!'
jokes.setup: Frank is informed he's been in his office for three months
jokes.punchline: His reaction is not horror at losing three months of his life but ecstasy — 'I'm gonna be a billionaire!' — the game is so good he sees it as a business opportunity
jokes.explanation: Frank's pivot from 'lost three months of his life' to 'business opportunity' is excellent character comedy. He's not horrified — he's validated. The final exclamation is a great episode button for the Tracy/Frank/Goregasm storyline.

tmdb_overview: In the second season finale, Jack moves on to a new job involving politics in Washington, but the position is not quite what he anticipated. Meanwhile, Liz suffers a pregnancy scare, Kenneth confronts rival page Donny when applying for a summer job, and Tracy works on his latest invention.
insight: Elite density carries absurdist escalation: 63 jokes in 22 minutes sustains 94+ rating.
